instructions: Make the tangzhong first. In a small saucepan, off the heat, whisk 2 tbsp of the bread flour into 1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp of the milk until there are no lumps.
Set the pan over low heat and whisk the whole time. After a few minutes it turns into a thick paste, and it's ready when the whisk leaves lines that stay put.
Transfer the paste into a small bowl and let it cool to room temperature, about 15 minutes. If you're making it the night before, cover it and keep it in the fridge.
Warm 1/2 cup of the milk until it feels just warm on your wrist, about 98°F. Twenty seconds in the microwave does it.
Put the remaining 2 1/3 cups bread flour, the yeast, the salt and 1/4 cup sugar into the bowl of a stand mixer and stir them together. Add 1 of the eggs and the cooled tangzhong.
Fit the dough hook and mix on low. Slowly pour in the warm milk until a sticky dough comes together.
Add the butter 1 tbsp at a time, and wait until each piece has disappeared into the dough before the next one goes in.

Knead on medium speed for 10 to 15 minutes, until the dough pulls away from the sides of the bowl. Pinch off a small piece and stretch it. If it forms a thin sheet you can nearly see through, it's ready. The dough stays tacky, and that's right.
Rub the oil around a large clean bowl. Shape the dough into a smooth ball and put it in the bowl. Cover it and leave it somewhere warm for about 1 hour, until it has doubled in size.
Transfer the dough onto the counter and cut it into 2 equal pieces. Roll each into a ball, cover them with a clean towel and rest them for 20 minutes.
Roll one ball into a rectangle about 6 by 8 inches. Fold the right end into the center, then the left end into the center. Turn it so a short side faces you and roll it up tightly, away from you.
Place the roll at one end of an 8.5 by 4.5 inch loaf pan with the seam toward the middle of the pan. Shape the second ball the same way and set it beside the first.
Cover the pan and leave it somewhere warm for 30 to 45 minutes, until the dough has risen to the top of the pan.
Meanwhile, heat the oven to 350°F with a rack in the lower middle and an empty baking sheet on it. Beat the second egg with the last 1 tbsp milk.

Brush the egg mixture over the top of both rolls. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until the loaf is golden. You're baking it to 185°F in the middle, so if you have a thermometer, check it there. No thermometer? The top should be deep golden and sound hollow when you tap it.
Leave the loaf in the pan for 5 minutes, then transfer it onto a wire rack. Let it cool for at least 1 hour before slicing.
Slice the loaf. Keep what you'll eat in the next 3 days in an airtight container on the counter, or up to 1 week in the fridge. Freeze the rest in a freezer container for up to 3 months.
To eat, toast a slice until golden. Frozen slices go straight into the toaster.
advance_prep_notes: Bake the loaf on the weekend. The whole bake takes about 3 hours, and the slices keep for a week of toast.
method_notes: Both of the readable versions start with a tangzhong, a cooked flour and milk paste, and add it to an egg and butter enriched dough that is kneaded until it passes the windowpane test. Eat Little Bird divides the dough in two and bakes it at 350°F; Sift & Simmer uses a larger Pullman loaf with a lid, three pieces and more yeast. Eat Little Bird does not give storage times, so the keeping times (3 days on the counter, 1 week in the fridge, 3 months frozen, toast from frozen) come from Sift & Simmer. Every readable version has fewer than 20 ratings (5 from 7, 5 from 3 and 5 from 2), so this is a fallback lead. RecipeTin Japan, the trusted cook for Japanese food, has no shokupan recipe yet.
